title: Stakeholder expectations: SLAs, limits and pilot feedback
titleVi: Kỳ vọng của các bên liên quan: SLA, giới hạn và phản hồi từ triển khai thử nghiệm

units.text: Manage stakeholder feedback loops and expectation alignment
What you will be able to do
State what the standard and Priority service tiers promise about availability, and what they leave out
Explain how organisation rate limits and spend caps limit throughput and cost, and recognise each error a stakeholder will see
Collect the model-selection criteria stakeholders should sign off before an SLA, and reopen them after launch
Name the right channels for Anthropic-side incidents and for model retirement notices, including how partner platforms differ
Set up a pilot feedback loop that collects, triages and reports back from day one
Tell a real quality drop from normal variation before reacting to a complaint
Key concept
Ceilings and targets, not guarantees

The service-level facts a Claude deployment relies on are maximums and targets: rate limits and spend caps cap usage without promising capacity, and only Priority Tier comes with an uptime target. Any expectation you set with stakeholders has to be built on these ceilings, not on numbers nobody is committed to.
In this lesson

What standard and Priority Tier actually promise

Stakeholders rarely ask about service tiers directly. They ask "will it be up?", and the honest answer depends on which tier the traffic runs on. Anthropic offers three tiers. Standard is the default for every API request. Priority Tier needs an existing capacity commitment. Batch is for asynchronous work that can wait. Promising availability you have not paid for is the most common way an SLA conversation goes wrong later.
Standard
promises best effort and nothing more. Its requests are prioritised alongside everyone else's, so a busy period can return "server overloaded" errors and there is no uptime figure to quote.
Priority Tier

puts your requests ahead of all other traffic, which helps minimise overload errors even at peak times, and it targets 99.5% uptime. Two words in that sentence matter. "Targets" is not "guarantees". And the target covers only the capacity you committed to: requests beyond it automatically fall back to standard tier.
What each service tier offers when you set availability expectations
Tier
Who gets it
What it promises
What it does not cover
Standard
Every request by default
Best-effort availability, prioritised alongside all other requests
No uptime target; overload errors are possible at peak
Priority Tier
Organisations with a capacity commitment
Targets 99.5% uptime with prioritised compute
Traffic above committed input/output tokens per minute falls back to standard
Batch
Asynchronous workflows
Work that can wait or run outside normal capacity
Not for interactive, latency-sensitive paths
A Priority Tier commitment is specific. It names input tokens per minute, output tokens per minute, a duration of 1, 3, 6 or 12 months, and
one specific model version

. Cache reads and writes, along with US-only inference on newer models, count against that capacity at their own weightings, so a heavily cached workload uses less commitment than its raw token count suggests. Check which model you plan to run before you promise Priority Tier. It is not supported on several current models, including Claude Fable 5.1, Claude Opus 5.5, Claude Sonnet 5.5 and Claude Haiku 5.5. A stakeholder who has been told "we'll get the 99.5% tier" for an Opus 5.5 workflow has been told something that cannot happen.
On the exam
An availability promise has three parts: which tier, which model version, and how much capacity. A 99.5% figure quoted without all three overstates what Priority Tier gives you.
Exam trap
Priority Tier guarantees 99.5% uptime for all of a customer's traffic, on any model.
Why is that wrong?

Rate limits and spend caps are ceilings
Two organisation-level limits set how much a deployment can do:
rate limits
cap requests and tokens per period, and
spend limits

cap monthly cost. Both come from your usage tier. Organisations are placed on a tier automatically from their usage history and move up over time, and new organisations may start in a lower Evaluation tier. These limits are enforced across the whole organisation. You can set lower limits of your own on individual workspaces, which is how one team's pilot is kept from using up another team's headroom.

Rate limits on the Messages API are measured per model class as requests per minute (RPM), input tokens per minute (ITPM) and output tokens per minute (OTPM). They are enforced over shorter windows than their names suggest. A 60 RPM limit can behave like one request per second, so a burst can fail even when the minute's total is under the limit. Caching is the lever to explain to stakeholders: for most models only uncached input tokens count toward ITPM, so a high cache hit rate raises effective throughput without a tier change. A higher limit can be requested in the Console once you are using at least 50% of your current limits.
Monthly spend cap by usage tier
Usage tier
Monthly spend cap

Predict first
On the 24th, a team's production traffic starts returning HTTP 429. The SDK is set to retry automatically. What happens next?
The API drops the requests to batch processing and finishes them later
The retries succeed within seconds, because a 429 always comes with a retry-after header
If the 429 is the tier spend cap, every retry fails until 00:00 UTC on the first of next month unless the organisation moves up a tier

Hitting the spend cap does not slow usage down. It stops it. When the organisation reaches its tier's cap, API usage pauses until 00:00 UTC on the first day of the next month. A limit you set yourself below the cap behaves differently again. Stakeholders should know in advance which of these three responses they could see and who is able to fix each one.

Exam traps
A rate limit is reserved capacity, so throughput up to the limit can be promised to stakeholders.
Why is that wrong?
Every 429 clears itself if the client keeps retrying.
Why is that wrong?
Checkpoint 2 of 9
Check yourself

Your organisation's usage tier gives a pilot team a high RPM and ITPM rate limit on the Messages API, and all of its traffic runs on the standard tier. The product owner wants to tell users that throughput up to that limit is assured. What can you honestly commit to?
Nothing beyond best effort: the rate limit is only a ceiling, and standard traffic gets best-effort availability unless a Priority Tier commitment covers it
Guaranteed throughput once a higher limit is requested in the Console, because a raised limit becomes reserved capacity
Throughput up to the rate limit, because the rate limit is capacity reserved for the organisation
Throughput up to the rate limit, provided the per-minute totals stay under the limit
Sources
Criteria stakeholders sign off before an SLA
An SLA is only as good as the criteria behind it. Write them so they can be measured, as covered in
Measurable success criteria

, and then have stakeholders sign them. The work in a sign-off session is turning "it should be fast and cheap" into choices stakeholders own. Choosing a Claude model means balancing three factors, and each one is a question to put to the business, not one for engineering to answer alone.
Ask these three questions in the session:
Capabilities:
which features the model must have to meet the workflow's functional requirements.
Speed:

how quickly the application must respond, and whether premium pricing is acceptable for it. Fast mode on Claude Opus 5.5, Claude Opus 5 and Claude Opus 4.8 delivers up to 2.5x higher output speed at premium pricing, which is a business decision.
Cost:
the budget for both development and production usage, which also sets the usage tier and spend cap you will need.

Architecture details such as parameter counts or where the weights are hosted are not selection criteria. Stakeholders can't evaluate them and the model guidance doesn't ask for them. Uptime and response time, on the other hand, belong in the signed criteria as operational metrics, worded as targets that match the tier you are actually buying.

Signed criteria need to be reopened after launch, because the model underneath them changes. Prompts and guardrails tuned for one model can hold back a more capable one, so teams retest tasks as models change and improve. An eval suite keeps that renegotiation honest. Early on it makes the team define what success means, and later it holds the system to a consistent quality bar. A request to relax latency in exchange for a stronger model, or to accept a new model after a retirement, is then decided against numbers rather than impressions.
Apply it to your own work
Think of a stakeholder wish you have heard recently, such as "it should feel instant". Which of capabilities, speed or cost does it really belong to, and what number would they need to sign?
Checkpoint 3 of 9
Check yourself

Six months after stakeholders signed the success criteria, the team moves the workflow to a newer, more capable Claude model and keeps the original prompts and guardrails. A stakeholder asks whether the signed criteria still hold. What should you do?
Rerun the eval suite against the signed criteria and retest the tasks, revising prompts and guardrails that may now hold the stronger model back
Collect user impressions for a few weeks, then reopen the criteria only if complaints rise
Keep the original prompts and guardrails unchanged, because they were tuned and signed off with the criteria
Treat the criteria as still met, because a more capable model can only do as well as or better than the one they were signed against
Checkpoint 4 of 9
Exam question

Before committing to an SLA for a new agentic workflow, a delivery lead wants to run a structured feedback session with business stakeholders to align on model selection criteria, following Anthropic's guidance on choosing a model. Which factors should the lead explicitly gather from stakeholders during this session? (Select all that apply)
(Select
The capabilities the model must support to meet the workflow's functional requirements
The speed and latency requirements the application needs, including whether premium fast-mode pricing is acceptable
The budget constraints for both development and production usage
The exact number of parameters in the underlying model architecture
Which specific data center rack the model's weights are physically stored on
Check answer
0 of 3 selected

How stakeholders hear about outages and model retirements
Every customer's incident runbook should name one public source for Anthropic-side incidents:
status.claude.com

. It gives real-time updates on the scope, impact and resolution progress of confirmed incidents. Account and billing questions go through a separate channel, Support, which you reach from the message icon in the Help Center or from "Get help" in the Claude Console. Keep the two apart in the handbook. One reports what is happening to everyone. The other handles your organisation's own case.

Some signals look like outages but are not. Capacity constraints, where demand is high but the system is working normally, do not appear on the status page, because they are normal load management. A 429 means your organisation hit a limit; it is not evidence of an incident. Internal dashboards, rate-limit charts and model system cards all have their uses, but none of them is where Anthropic announces incidents.

Model retirement is the other planned event that changes a committed timeline. Anthropic notifies affected customers by email and in the documentation, giving at least 60 days' notice before a publicly released model is retired. Deprecated models still work but have a replacement and a retirement date. Retired models fail every request. You can find which keys still call a deprecated model by exporting the Console Usage page as a CSV broken down by API key and model.
Predict first
A vendor runs one legacy component on a model that Anthropic has retired, with some traffic on the Claude API and some on Google Cloud. What expectation should they set for each?
Claude API traffic must migrate before the retirement date; Google Cloud traffic follows Google Cloud's own schedule
Neither is affected, because existing production traffic is exempt from retirement
Both stop together, because one retirement date applies on every platform

Which platform the traffic runs on decides which retirement date applies. Anthropic's published dates cover the Claude API, Claude Platform on AWS and Microsoft Foundry. Amazon Bedrock and Google Cloud run their own lifecycle, so the same model can be retired on the Claude API and still be available on a partner platform. Direct API traffic has to move to a supported model before Anthropic's date. Traffic on a partner platform follows that platform's timeline. Existing traffic gets no exemption, and retirement blocks API requests, not only the Console. How to run the migration itself is covered in
Lifecycle phases and model migration
Exam trap
An Anthropic retirement date applies on every hosting platform, including Amazon Bedrock and Google Cloud.
Why is that wrong?
Checkpoint 5 of 9
Check yourself

At peak hours, a pilot running on the standard tier starts returning "server overloaded" errors. The product owner wants to tell users that Anthropic is having an outage and point them to status.claude.com. What should you tell the product owner?
Open a Support case instead, because overload errors are an issue with your organisation's account and Support will post the outage notice
Go ahead: overload errors mean an Anthropic incident, and the status page will post an update shortly
Hold off: standard tier is best effort, so overload at peak is normal load management, not a confirmed incident, and it will not appear on the status page
Check the model system card and internal rate-limit charts, because that is where Anthropic announces capacity incidents
Checkpoint 6 of 9
Exam question

A customer support tooling vendor still runs Claude Haiku 3.5 in a legacy component and receives Anthropic's notice that the model is retired outside of Bedrock and Google Cloud. Their engineering stakeholders want to know how this affects their committed timeline. What is the accurate expectation to set?

Direct API and other non-Bedrock/Vertex-hosted traffic on Haiku 3.5 must migrate to a supported model before retirement, while deployments specifically on Bedrock or Google Cloud can keep running it under those platforms' own timelines
The retirement notice only affects new customers who sign up after the announcement date, so the vendor's existing production traffic is permanently exempt regardless of hosting platform
Retirement notices apply uniformly across every hosting platform including Bedrock and Google Cloud, so all deployments of Haiku 3.5 everywhere must migrate by the same date
Model retirement only restricts access to the Console UI for prompting Haiku 3.5, while direct Messages API traffic on any platform continues indefinitely unaffected
Checkpoint 7 of 9
Exam question

An account manager is drafting an incident-communication annex for a customer's stakeholder handbook, describing how they will learn about Anthropic-side outages affecting their production deployment. Which resource should the annex point to as the authoritative, real-time source, separate from the account-specific support channel?
status.claude.com, which reports current Anthropic service status, alongside the Help Center for account and billing questions
The customer's own internal monitoring dashboard, since Anthropic does not publish any public service status information
The model's system card, which is updated in real time whenever an incident affecting API availability occurs
The Claude Console's rate limit charts, since sustained 429 errors are the only reliable indicator of an Anthropic-side outage

Building the feedback loop into the pilot

Decide how feedback will be collected and used before the pilot starts. Feedback gathered as an afterthought arrives as scattered complaints with no context. The pilot invitation is the first part of the loop. Tell the cohort they were chosen because they will use it on real problems and tell you the truth about it. Then give them a specific request: use it on at least one real task, and post what worked, what was annoying and what surprised them. Close by telling them what their input is for, so they know it has consequences.

Collection needs one place and one owner. A single channel gives questions one place to land. Name an owner to watch it for the first 48 hours, because unanswered launch-day questions kill momentum. Answer in public so each answer benefits everyone watching. A weekly prompt keeps feedback coming without a meeting: each Friday, ask what the tool helped with this week, and accept screenshots or a couple of sentences.

Triage and reporting back keep the loop from becoming a suggestion box. Sort each item before acting on it. Is it a capability gap, a limit or quota problem, a prompt or configuration fix, or a quality complaint that needs checking against evals? Then report the outcome back to the people who raised it. Usage data adds a signal nobody has to type. Analytics show adoption trends and dips in usage that may indicate friction, which tells you where to ask questions. One Anthropic team kept the human side manageable with a weekly "lessons & missteps" report and by batching questions so a reviewer could answer them in one pass. Reviewer attention runs out, so the loop should use it carefully.

Stage

Output stakeholders see

Dedicated channel with a named owner; ask for what worked, what was annoying, what surprised
Every question has an answer, in public
Prompt
Weekly show-and-tell thread
A running record of real wins and failures
Observe
Usage analytics: active users, sessions, spend
Dips that flag friction before anyone complains

Weekly summary of decisions taken from feedback
Evidence that feedback decides the wider rollout

Separating real degradation from normal variation

"It feels worse this week" is the complaint every pilot gets eventually, and responding before checking is how teams lose a week. Without evals, debugging is reactive. You wait for complaints, reproduce them by hand, fix something, and hope nothing else regressed. The underlying problem is that a team without evals can't distinguish real regressions from noise. A model gives different answers to similar inputs, so a few bad outputs are not evidence that anything changed.
Three users report worse answers on Tuesday. Nothing is posted on status.claude.com, and the eval suite run against Tuesday's build scores the same as last week's. What do you tell the stakeholder?
Check causes in a fixed order, cheapest first:
Confirmed incident:
is there an active entry on status.claude.com? If so, the cause is outside your system and the status page tells you scope and progress.
Capacity or limits:
are errors overload responses or 429s? Capacity constraints are not outages, and limit errors appear in the table above. Neither is a quality problem.
Measured regression:
does the eval suite, run on the current build, score below its baseline? Only this result justifies a rollback or a prompt change.
Normal variation:
if none of the above applies, add the reported examples to the eval set and tell the stakeholder what you measured.

Set the expectation for variation in the signed criteria, before anyone complains. Consistency is a criterion of its own: how similar responses need to be for similar inputs, and how much it matters that the same question asked twice gets a semantically similar answer. A stakeholder who signed "answers may vary in wording but not in substance" has a standard to judge a complaint against. Without one, every unexpected answer looks like a regression.
Exam trap
A capacity-constraint message means Anthropic is having an outage, and it will be on the status page.
Why is that wrong?
Checkpoint 9 of 9
Check yourself

On Wednesday, after a prompt change shipped on Monday, several pilot users say answers "feel worse". status.claude.com shows no active incident, and there are no overload errors or 429s. The team lead wants to roll back Monday's prompt change straight away. What should decide whether you roll back?
Running the eval suite on the current build and comparing it with the baseline, then rolling back only if the score has dropped
The number of complaints: if several users report the same thing, the change caused a regression and should be rolled back
A Support case: Anthropic can confirm whether model quality changed for your organisation this week
Reproducing the reported prompts by hand: if any of them gives a bad answer again, roll back the change
